newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.African cries as he confronts his wife's killers.
newsitem.headline: S.African cries as he confronts his wife's killers.

text.p: A white South African who watched black guerrillas kill his wife in an attack on a church congregation wept on Thursday when he confronted them at a hearing of the country's truth commission.

Dawie Ackerman, whose wife was one of 11 people killed in the raid in July 1993, told the three men -- who are applying for amnesty from the Truth and Reconciliation Commission -- that he forgave them.
Ackerman originally opposed the amnesty application but when he was called to give evidence he told the men in an emotional outburst:

"I want you to know that I forgive you unconditionally. I do that because I am a Christian, and I can forgive you for the hurt you have caused me, but I cannot forgive you the sin you have done. Only God can forgive you for that."
In testimony frequently interrupted as he struggled to control his sobbing, Ackerman said:
"I have a need to say it. I want them to hear it... I've never cried for my wife, other than to have silent cries. I've never had an emotional crying outburst."
Addressing his lawyer, Ackerman said he had sympathised with one of the three guerrillas who had described his own pain and suffering from the witness stand.
"I wrote you a note to bring your cross-examination to an end. Just what are we doing here? The truth, yes.
"But I looked at the way in which he answered you, and his anger, how on earth are we going to be reconciled?"

The truth commission, chaired by Archbishop Desmond Tutu, has powers to grant amnesty to those who confess fully to their deeds during the apartheid era. Applicants have to convince the commission that their motives were political and that their actions were carried out with a sense of proportion.
The men appearing on Thursday said they were members of the armed wing of the radical Pan Africanist Congress and believed the Cape Town church they attacked was a legitimate target.
The commission, whose aim is to reconcile through revealing the truth of human rights abuses, has yet to rule on their application.
